questions.question: What is a Spring Boot starter dependency?
questions.title: What are Spring Boot starters?
questions.direct_answer: A Spring Boot starter is a dependency descriptor for a particular job, such as building a web application or using JPA. Adding one starter brings the related libraries as transitive dependencies. Spring Boot's dependency management supplies versions for managed libraries, while auto-configuration is a separate feature that reacts to the resulting classpath.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can separate a starter, dependency management, and auto-configuration instead of treating them as one feature.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling a starter a large bundle of copied classes or claiming that the starter itself chooses every version and creates beans.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use one dependency graph to show what the starter declares, what the Boot BOM manages, and what auto-configuration later detects.

sections.title: Starter, Dependency Management, and Auto-configuration
sections.content:
A starter is a small Maven or Gradle dependency whose main purpose is to declare a useful set of other dependencies. For a servlet web application, `spring-boot-starter-web` brings Spring MVC, JSON support, and the default embedded Tomcat server. The starter saves the developer from finding and declaring those pieces one by one.

Three related ideas do different jobs. The **starter** selects a convenient dependency set. Spring Boot's **dependency management** supplies recommended versions for managed coordinates when the project inherits from `spring-boot-starter-parent`, imports the `spring-boot-dependencies` BOM, or configures equivalent Gradle support. **Auto-configuration** runs later: it examines the classes and beans that are present and may configure an MVC application, a JSON mapper, or an embedded server. Adding a starter often makes auto-configuration conditions true, but the starter does not itself create those beans.

The web starter is a useful example. Its POM declares other artifacts, so the build tool expands one direct dependency into a graph. Maven or Gradle still resolves that graph using normal dependency rules. A direct declaration of a library already present transitively is not automatically a duplicate JAR; it may simply document direct use or affect version selection. An explicit version can override Boot's managed recommendation, so such overrides should be deliberate and tested.

A starter also does not cover every possible library. If an artifact is outside Boot's managed set, it still needs an explicit version. The practical habit is to add the starter that matches the feature, inspect the resolved graph, and add individual dependencies only when the application uses them directly or needs a feature the starter does not provide.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: A starter declares a convenient set of dependencies for one kind of application feature.
The Boot parent, BOM, or configured Gradle support manages versions; the starter is not the version-management mechanism by itself.
Auto-configuration is separate and reacts to the classes and beans that the dependency graph puts on the classpath.
Individual dependencies are still valid when the code uses them directly or when the starter does not provide them.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A Spring Boot starter is a dependency descriptor for a particular capability. Instead of declaring Spring MVC, Jackson, an embedded servlet container, and their supporting libraries one by one, a web application can declare `spring-boot-starter-web`. Maven or Gradle then follows that starter's transitive dependency graph.

The starter is only one part of the arrangement. Boot's dependency management supplies recommended versions for managed libraries, while auto-configuration checks the resulting classpath and existing beans at application startup. In the web example, the starter makes MVC and Tomcat classes available; separate auto-configuration can then create the usual web infrastructure when its conditions match.

A starter is therefore more than a short name, but it is not a JAR containing every library and it does not guarantee that any mixture of overrides is compatible. If I add a versioned Jackson dependency myself, normal Maven or Gradle resolution decides which version is used. If I add an unmanaged library, I provide its version.

I normally begin with the relevant starter, keep Boot's managed versions unless there is a tested reason to change one, and inspect the resolved graph with `mvn dependency:tree` or the Gradle dependency report when the classpath is unclear. The final resolved tree, not the starter name alone, is the runtime classpath and the reliable place to check what the application received.

sections.title: A Web Starter and Its Resolved Graph
sections.content:
```xml
<parent>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>3.3.1</version>
</parent>

<properties>
    <java.version>17</java.version>
</properties>

<dependencies>
    <dependency>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    </dependency>
</dependencies>
```

Running `mvn dependency:tree` shows `spring-webmvc`, `spring-boot-starter-json`, and `spring-boot-starter-tomcat` below the one direct web-starter declaration in the Boot 3.3.1 graph. Their versions are omitted from this POM because the parent supplies dependency management.

sections.title: Where the Mental Model Breaks
sections.content:
- **Calling the starter a fat JAR**: the starter mainly declares dependencies; the build tool fetches the real library JARs.
- **Giving the starter every job**: dependency management chooses managed versions and auto-configuration creates application infrastructure.
- **Assuming a direct dependency creates two copies**: resolution normally selects one version of a module; the real risk is an unintended override or an inconsistent graph.
- **Omitting every version blindly**: only coordinates covered by configured dependency management can omit a version.

questions.question: What are the most commonly used Spring Boot starters?
questions.title: Common Spring Boot starters and what they provide
questions.direct_answer: The most commonly used Spring Boot starters are `spring-boot-starter-web` for Spring MVC applications, `data-jpa` for JPA access, `validation` for Jakarta Bean Validation, `security` for Spring Security, `actuator` for production-ready management features, and `test` for common test libraries. They are examples, not a fixed checklist; each application should include only the capabilities it uses.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate recognises real starter coordinates and can connect each one to a concrete responsibility.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Memorising invented names or describing every common starter as mandatory for every project.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Build one small service dependency list and explain why the database driver and validation starter are separate choices.

sections.title: Common Starters by Application Responsibility
sections.content:
Spring Boot has many starters, so the useful way to learn them is by the job they support. `spring-boot-starter-web` is the common entry point for a servlet web application using Spring MVC and, by default, embedded Tomcat. `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` adds Spring Data JPA, Hibernate, and JDBC-related infrastructure, but it does not select a database vendor or JDBC driver.

`spring-boot-starter-validation` adds Hibernate Validator so Jakarta constraints such as `@NotBlank` and `@Size` can be enforced. It is a separate dependency in Boot 3.3.1; adding the web starter alone does not provide it. `spring-boot-starter-security` supplies Spring Security modules. In a web application, Boot's security auto-configuration can establish a default security setup when its conditions match, but a real service still needs an intentional authorization design.

`spring-boot-starter-actuator` adds production-ready management features, including health and metrics infrastructure. Exposure is configurable: the presence of Actuator does not mean every endpoint is publicly available. `spring-boot-starter-test` belongs in test scope and supplies Boot's test support plus widely used libraries such as JUnit Jupiter, AssertJ, Hamcrest, Mockito, and Spring Test in the Boot 3.3.1 dependency graph.

Consider an order API. It may need web, validation, data-jpa, a PostgreSQL driver, actuator, and test. Security belongs there only if that service owns an authentication or authorization boundary. A command-line batch program may need data-jpa and validation but no web starter at all. Starters are chosen from requirements, not added as a standard six-item package.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Web: Spring MVC and default embedded Tomcat for servlet applications.
Data JPA: repositories and JPA infrastructure; add the database's JDBC driver separately.
Validation and Security: input constraints and security libraries are separate capabilities.
Actuator: management features such as health and metrics infrastructure, with configurable exposure.
Test: common testing support and libraries, declared in test scope.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
The commonly used starters depend on the kind of service. For a normal servlet REST API, `spring-boot-starter-web` supplies Spring MVC, JSON support, and Tomcat as the default embedded server. For persistence, `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` supplies Spring Data JPA and Hibernate, while the PostgreSQL or MySQL JDBC driver is added separately.

Input validation comes from `spring-boot-starter-validation`, which provides Jakarta Bean Validation through Hibernate Validator. `spring-boot-starter-security` supplies Spring Security for authentication and authorization work. `spring-boot-starter-actuator` supplies management features such as health and metrics infrastructure, and `spring-boot-starter-test` supplies Boot test support together with common testing libraries; the test starter should be limited to the test classpath.

An order service is a practical example. I might choose web for controllers, validation for request DTO rules, data-jpa plus the PostgreSQL driver for storage, actuator for operational health, and test for automated tests. I would add security only when the service's security requirements call for it.

The important boundary is that a starter does not finish the feature by itself: JPA still needs a database and mapping design, security still needs rules, and Actuator endpoint exposure still needs configuration. The correct list is therefore requirement-driven rather than a fixed set that every Boot project must contain.

sections.content:

|---|---|---|

sections.title: Starter Selection Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Inventing artifact names**: use the official coordinates, such as `starter-data-jpa`, rather than guessed names such as `starter-database`.
- **Expecting web to include validation**: in Boot 3.3.1, validation is a separate starter.
- **Expecting data-jpa to include PostgreSQL or MySQL**: the application chooses and adds its driver.
- **Treating Actuator as automatically public**: management endpoint availability and exposure are separate settings.
- **Putting starter-test on the production classpath**: Maven `test` scope or Gradle `testImplementation` keeps test libraries out of normal runtime use.

A real project includes only the capabilities it uses and still configures each feature deliberately.

questions.question: What does spring-boot-starter-test include, and what is @SpringBootTest?
questions.title: spring-boot-starter-test and @SpringBootTest
questions.direct_answer: In Boot 3.3.1, `spring-boot-starter-test` supplies Boot and Spring test support plus common libraries including JUnit Jupiter, AssertJ, Hamcrest, Mockito, JSON testing tools, and XMLUnit. `@SpringBootTest` is an integration-test annotation that finds Boot configuration and loads an application context; its default `MOCK` web environment does not start a listening server.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate separates a test dependency bundle from the annotation that loads a Boot application context.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest for every test or claiming that it always starts a real server and rebuilds a new context for every class.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Match plain unit tests, focused test slices, and full-context tests to the behavior being proved, and mention context caching.

sections.title: Test Libraries and Test Context Scope
sections.content:
`spring-boot-starter-test` is a test dependency, not a testing strategy. In the Boot 3.3.1 dependency graph it brings `spring-boot-test`, `spring-boot-test-autoconfigure`, Spring Test, JUnit Jupiter, AssertJ, Hamcrest, Mockito, JSON-path and JSON assertion support, Awaitility, and XMLUnit, among other supporting artifacts. The exact graph can change between Boot releases, so the build's dependency report is the final source for a project.

`@SpringBootTest` answers a different question: how much of the application should a test load? It uses Boot's test context support to locate the application's `@SpringBootConfiguration`, normally the class annotated with `@SpringBootApplication`, and creates an `ApplicationContext`. Beans, configuration properties, and auto-configuration can therefore take part in the test. The default `webEnvironment = MOCK` creates a web application context when appropriate but does not open a network port. `RANDOM_PORT` or `DEFINED_PORT` starts an embedded server.

An order total calculation needs no Spring context if it is ordinary Java logic. A controller serialization or MVC binding test can use `@WebMvcTest`, and a repository mapping test can use `@DataJpaTest`. A full order-placement test that needs configuration, validation, repositories, and transaction behavior may justify `@SpringBootTest`. This is a scope decision, not a rule that integration tests are automatically better.

Full contexts cost more to create than plain objects. Spring's TestContext framework caches contexts and reuses one when later tests have the same configuration, so it is inaccurate to say that every test class always boots a fresh copy. Different profiles, properties, mock-bean arrangements, or dirty-context markers can create different cache keys. Keeping test configuration consistent helps the cache do useful work.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: starter-test supplies the test toolkit; @SpringBootTest controls full Boot context loading.
Boot 3.3.1 includes JUnit Jupiter, Mockito, AssertJ, Hamcrest, Spring Test, and additional JSON/XML test tools.
The default @SpringBootTest web environment is MOCK, so no real server listens on a port.
Use RANDOM_PORT when the test must cross a real HTTP boundary.
Spring can reuse matching application contexts through the TestContext cache.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`spring-boot-starter-test` is the usual test-scoped dependency for a Boot project. In Boot 3.3.1 it brings Boot's test modules and Spring Test, together with JUnit Jupiter, Mockito, AssertJ, Hamcrest, and several JSON and XML testing tools. It gives the project libraries; it does not mean every test must load Spring.

`@SpringBootTest` is used when a test needs the Boot application context. It finds the main Boot configuration and loads beans and auto-configuration much like the application. By default it uses the `MOCK` web environment, so it does not start a listening server. `RANDOM_PORT` is the choice when the test must make a real HTTP call to an embedded server.

For an order service, I would test a price calculator with plain JUnit and Mockito because it is ordinary Java logic. I would use `@WebMvcTest` for controller mapping and JSON behavior, `@DataJpaTest` for repository mapping, and `@SpringBootTest` for a flow that genuinely needs several layers and Boot configuration together.

A plain `@Mock` creates a Mockito object for the test; it does not replace an existing bean in the application context. In Boot 3.3.1, `@MockBean` can replace a bean for a Spring test. Full contexts are heavier, although Spring caches and reuses contexts with matching configuration, so careful test scope and consistent configuration both matter. That balance keeps fast feedback for local logic without losing integration coverage where framework wiring is part of the requirement.

sections.content:
| Test style | Loads Spring? | Suitable order-service check |
|---|---|---|
| JUnit + Mockito | No | Price or discount logic |
| `@WebMvcTest` | MVC slice | Route, binding, validation response, JSON |
| `@DataJpaTest` | JPA slice | Entity mapping and repository query |
| `@SpringBootTest` | Full Boot context | Several configured layers working together |
| `@SpringBootTest(RANDOM_PORT)` | Full context and server | Real HTTP request through the embedded server |

sections.title: A Full-context Order Placement Check
Testing Scope Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Annotating every class with `@SpringBootTest`**: pure calculations and small collaborators can be tested without a container.
- **Assuming a real server always starts**: the default is `MOCK`; choose `RANDOM_PORT` for an actual socket.
- **Claiming each test always creates a new context**: matching TestContext configurations can reuse the cached context.
- **Using `@Mock` to replace an application bean**: a local Mockito mock does not alter the Spring context.
- **Treating the starter's current library list as permanent**: inspect the selected Boot version's resolved graph.

questions.question: How do you add a database driver dependency alongside spring-boot-starter-data-jpa?
questions.title: Adding a database driver with spring-boot-starter-data-jpa
questions.direct_answer: Add `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` plus the JDBC driver for the chosen database. For PostgreSQL, use `org.postgresql:postgresql`, commonly with Maven `runtime` scope or Gradle `runtimeOnly` when source code uses only standard JPA/JDBC APIs. Configure the datasource URL and authentication outside source code; Boot can usually infer the driver class from the JDBC URL.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands that JPA infrastructure and a vendor JDBC driver are separate dependencies.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding only data-jpa, hardcoding secrets, or repeating a driver-class name that Boot can infer from the URL.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why runtime scope is common rather than universal, and distinguish an external database from an embedded test database.

sections.title: JPA Infrastructure and the Database Driver
sections.content:
`spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` provides the Spring Data repository layer, Hibernate, and JDBC-related infrastructure. It cannot decide whether the application uses PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, or an embedded database. The vendor's JDBC driver is the code that understands that database's wire protocol, so it is a separate dependency.

For a PostgreSQL order service, the build declares both `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` and `org.postgresql:postgresql`. Maven `runtime` scope or Gradle `runtimeOnly` is common because application source normally imports `jakarta.persistence`, Spring Data, or standard JDBC types rather than PostgreSQL classes. That scope is not a law: if production code directly imports a vendor-specific class, the driver must also be available at compile time.

The application then needs a connection target. For an external database, `spring.datasource.url` identifies the JDBC URL, and credentials are commonly supplied through environment-specific configuration or a secret store. Boot can infer the driver class for most databases from the URL, so `spring.datasource.driver-class-name` is usually unnecessary. If no URL is provided, Boot tries to configure a supported embedded database when one is on the classpath; that is why URL and credentials are not universal requirements for every possible setup.

In the order example, the PostgreSQL driver being present lets Boot create a pooled `DataSource` when the other conditions and configuration are present. JPA then builds the `EntityManagerFactory` on top of that datasource. Schema ownership is a separate decision. In a maintained service, a migration tool such as Flyway or Liquibase normally owns production schema changes; `ddl-auto=validate` can check that entity mappings match the migrated schema without changing it.

Tests should also make the database choice explicit. H2 is useful for fast isolated checks, but its SQL and transaction behavior is not identical to PostgreSQL. A test that must prove PostgreSQL-specific mappings or queries should run against PostgreSQL, often through a disposable test container.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: data-jpa supplies JPA and repository infrastructure, not a vendor JDBC driver.
Add the PostgreSQL, MySQL, or other driver that matches the real database.
runtime/runtimeOnly is common when production code imports only standard APIs; vendor imports require compile visibility.
Boot normally infers the driver class from the JDBC URL.
Keep credentials outside the committed application source.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` gives the application Spring Data JPA, Hibernate, and the supporting JDBC infrastructure, but it does not choose a database vendor. I add the JDBC driver separately. For PostgreSQL, that is `org.postgresql:postgresql`; Boot's dependency management covers its version in a Boot 3.3.1 project.

The driver is commonly Maven `runtime` scope or Gradle `runtimeOnly` because application code normally works with JPA and standard JDBC types and only needs the vendor implementation while running. If the source directly imports a PostgreSQL-specific class, compile scope or `implementation` is required instead. For an external database I provide `spring.datasource.url` and authentication through environment-specific configuration or a secret source. Boot can usually infer the driver class from the JDBC URL.

For an order service, `jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/orders` selects PostgreSQL. Once the driver and connection settings are available, Boot can create the `DataSource`, and JPA uses it through the entity manager. I keep schema migration separate, usually with Flyway or Liquibase, and may use `ddl-auto=validate` to detect a mapping mismatch.

An embedded database can work without an explicit external URL, so URL, username, and password should not be described as three universal properties. I also use PostgreSQL-backed integration tests when database-specific behavior matters instead of assuming H2 is identical. That choice keeps the Java code portable while testing the database contract that production actually uses.

questions.question: What is spring-boot-starter-validation and how is it used?
questions.title: spring-boot-starter-validation and Bean Validation
questions.direct_answer: `spring-boot-starter-validation` is the starter that adds Hibernate Validator, the Jakarta Bean Validation implementation used by Boot 3.3.1. Put constraints such as `@NotBlank`, `@Email`, and `@Size` on input fields, then use `@Valid` on an MVC request body to validate the converted object. Invalid request bodies normally produce a 400 response before the controller method body runs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can explain constraints, the validation trigger, failure handling, and the difference between request validation and database integrity.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding annotations to a DTO without using the MVC validation entry point, or assuming @Email also rejects null and blank values.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show one request flowing through JSON conversion and validation, then keep the API error shape and database constraints as separate concerns.

sections.title: Constraints, Validation, and API Errors
sections.content:
`spring-boot-starter-validation` provides Hibernate Validator and the Jakarta Bean Validation API used by a Boot 3.3.1 application. A constraint annotation describes one rule close to the data it protects. `@NotBlank` requires non-null text with at least one non-whitespace character, `@Size` limits the size of a string or collection, and `@Email` checks an email-shaped value. `@Email` treats null as valid, so a required email normally combines `@NotBlank` and `@Email`.

For an MVC request body, Jackson first converts JSON into a Java object. `@Valid` on the `@RequestBody` parameter asks Spring MVC to validate that object. If a field fails, MVC raises `MethodArgumentNotValidException`; the normal result is a 400 response and the controller method body is not called. A `@RestControllerAdvice` is optional, but it is useful when the API needs a stable field-error format instead of the application's default error body.

Consider user registration. The DTO requires a name, a valid nonblank email, and a password of at least eight characters. A request with a blank name and short password fails at the HTTP boundary. The controller receives only a valid `RegistrationRequest`, which keeps repeated manual `if` checks out of each endpoint. Nested objects require cascading validation: mark the nested field with `@Valid` when its own constraints must be checked.

Validation annotations do not replace business rules or database constraints. `@Email` cannot prove that the user owns the address, and a uniqueness check normally belongs in the service/database flow. A `NOT NULL` or unique database constraint still protects data written from another endpoint, a migration, or another application instance.

Method validation is another entry point. When the validation implementation is present, Boot supports method constraints on managed beans; the target class uses Spring's `@Validated` so its constrained methods are checked. This is different from `@Valid`, which performs cascaded validation of an object graph.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: The validation starter supplies Jakarta Bean Validation through Hibernate Validator.
Constraints describe rules; @Valid triggers validation of an MVC request-body object.
Invalid request bodies normally become 400 responses before controller logic runs.
Use @Valid on nested fields when validation should continue into that object.
Bean Validation complements business checks and database constraints; it does not replace them.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`spring-boot-starter-validation` adds the Jakarta Bean Validation API and Hibernate Validator implementation used by Boot 3.3.1. I place constraints on an input model: `@NotBlank` for required text, `@Size` for length, and `@Email` for email format. A required email needs both `@NotBlank` and `@Email` because `@Email` alone allows null.

In a Spring MVC controller, `@Valid` on a `@RequestBody` tells MVC to validate the object after JSON conversion. For a registration request, a blank name or seven-character password fails before the controller method body runs. Spring raises `MethodArgumentNotValidException` and normal MVC handling returns 400. If the API needs a stable list of field errors, a `@RestControllerAdvice` can map that exception to the chosen response contract.

The boundary is important. Bean Validation checks the rules expressed by constraints; it does not prove email ownership, perform every business check, or protect the database from all other writers. I still enforce important integrity rules in the service and database.

For nested request objects I put `@Valid` on the nested field so validation cascades. For constraints on Spring-managed service method parameters or return values, `@Validated` at the class level enables that separate method-validation path. This keeps simple structural rules declarative while leaving business decisions in the correct layer. It also keeps each rule testable at the boundary where that rule belongs.

questions.question: What is the difference between spring-boot-starter-web and spring-boot-starter-webflux?
questions.title: starter-web vs starter-webflux
questions.direct_answer: `spring-boot-starter-web` is the servlet stack built around Spring MVC with embedded Tomcat by default, whereas `spring-boot-starter-webflux` is the reactive stack built around Reactor with Reactor Netty by default. WebFlux helps when work is non-blocking across the request path; adding reactive return types around blocking JPA work does not remove the blocking call.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the servlet and reactive programming models and can choose based on the full I/O path.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling WebFlux universally faster, claiming it always runs only on Netty, or saying the two starters cannot coexist.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain Boot's MVC preference when both starters are present and use one database-backed endpoint to show why downstream I/O matters.

sections.title: Servlet and Reactive Web Stacks
sections.content:
`spring-boot-starter-web` is the usual starter for a servlet application. It brings Spring MVC and uses embedded Tomcat by default in Boot 3.3.1. Controller methods commonly return ordinary objects, and servlet request processing works naturally with blocking libraries such as JDBC and JPA. This makes MVC a straightforward fit for many business and CRUD services.

`spring-boot-starter-webflux` brings Spring WebFlux, Reactor, and Reactor Netty as its default server. Reactive handlers commonly return `Mono` for zero or one result and `Flux` for zero or many results. The runtime can continue processing other work while a non-blocking database or HTTP client waits for I/O, rather than tying up a request thread for that wait. WebFlux can also run on a supported servlet container, so WebFlux and Netty are not the same concept.

The important word is **end to end**. Suppose an inventory endpoint reads a product from a relational database. An MVC controller calling a JPA repository performs a blocking database call in the servlet model. A WebFlux controller calling an R2DBC repository can keep that path reactive. If the WebFlux handler calls the same blocking JPA repository on an event-loop thread, wrapping the result in `Mono` does not make the database driver non-blocking. Blocking work can be isolated on another scheduler, but that adds operational and programming complexity and should be explicit.

The dependencies may coexist. Boot documents that when both web and webflux starters are present, it auto-configures Spring MVC by default; a common reason is using reactive `WebClient` inside an MVC application. A project can explicitly choose a reactive application type, but it should not assume that adding the second starter silently converts the whole application.

Neither stack is automatically faster. Workload, downstream libraries, team experience, latency, resource limits, and failure behavior all matter. MVC is often the simpler match for blocking persistence. WebFlux is valuable for streaming, long-lived connections, gateways, or high levels of concurrent waiting when the important I/O clients are also non-blocking.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: starter-web: Spring MVC on the Servlet API, with Tomcat as Boot's default embedded server.
starter-webflux: Spring WebFlux with Reactor, with Reactor Netty as the default server.
Reactive types do not turn a blocking JDBC or JPA call into non-blocking I/O.
When both starters are present, Boot normally auto-configures Spring MVC.
Select the stack from the whole request path and workload, not from a universal speed claim.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
`spring-boot-starter-web` gives a servlet application Spring MVC and uses embedded Tomcat by default. It fits naturally with ordinary controller return values and blocking dependencies such as JDBC and JPA. `spring-boot-starter-webflux` gives the reactive Spring WebFlux stack, Reactor types such as `Mono` and `Flux`, and Reactor Netty as the default server, although WebFlux can also run on supported servlet containers.

For an inventory lookup, an MVC controller can call a JPA repository and wait in the servlet model. A WebFlux controller can call an R2DBC repository and return a `Mono<Product>` without blocking the reactive I/O path. Putting the blocking JPA call inside `Mono.just` does not change the JDBC driver, and doing that work on an event-loop thread can harm the application. Blocking work can be isolated deliberately, but a mixed model is not free.

I choose MVC for a typical CRUD service whose libraries and database access are blocking. I consider WebFlux for streaming, gateway work, long-lived connections, or many concurrent operations that mostly wait on non-blocking I/O. I do not call WebFlux universally faster. The two starters can also coexist: Boot normally selects MVC when both are present, which supports the common case of using `WebClient` from an MVC application. If the application must be reactive, that choice should be explicit and the downstream clients should support it.

sections.content:
| Area | `starter-web` | `starter-webflux` |
|---|---|---|
| Programming model | Servlet, usually imperative | Reactive streams with Reactor |
| Default embedded server | Tomcat | Reactor Netty |
| Common return style | Plain value, collection, response type | `Mono<T>` or `Flux<T>` |
| Natural database match | JDBC and JPA | R2DBC or another reactive driver |
| Strong fit | Conventional business and CRUD APIs | Streaming or high concurrent waiting on non-blocking I/O |
| Important boundary | Blocking calls occupy execution resources | Blocking calls must be avoided or isolated deliberately |

Web Stack Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating WebFlux as a faster MVC**: it is a different programming and execution model.
- **Wrapping a blocking call in a publisher**: the wrapper does not change the database or HTTP client's I/O behavior.
- **Saying WebFlux requires Netty**: Reactor Netty is Boot's default, but supported servlet containers can host WebFlux.
- **Saying the starters cannot coexist**: Boot normally selects MVC when both are present.
- **Using numeric connection thresholds as rules**: measure the actual workload, dependencies, and resource limits.

questions.question: How do you exclude a transitive dependency from a Spring Boot starter?
questions.title: Excluding transitive dependencies from starters
questions.direct_answer: First identify which direct dependency brings the unwanted module. In Maven, put an `<exclusion>` for its group and artifact inside that dependency; in Gradle, attach `exclude` to that dependency declaration. An exclusion blocks only that dependency path, so verify the resolved graph and add a supported replacement when the removed module supplied required behavior.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands path-scoped dependency exclusions and can verify an exclude-and-replace change.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Removing a module from one path and assuming it is absent everywhere, or excluding the embedded server without adding a replacement.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use a Tomcat-to-Jetty swap, show both Maven and Gradle syntax, and verify the final runtime graph.

sections.title: Path-scoped Exclusion and Replacement
sections.content:
A transitive dependency arrives through another dependency. In Boot 3.3.1, `spring-boot-starter-web` brings `spring-boot-starter-tomcat`, which in turn brings Tomcat modules. If a servlet application has decided to use Jetty, the build must stop Tomcat from arriving through the web-starter path and add `spring-boot-starter-jetty` as the replacement.

In Maven, an exclusion sits inside the direct dependency that introduces the unwanted artifact. It names `groupId` and `artifactId`, not a version. The rule applies to that branch of the graph. If another direct or transitive dependency also reaches the same artifact, that second path can keep it in the resolved classpath. Maven's `dependency:tree` shows both the path before the change and the selected graph after it.

Gradle also supports a per-dependency exclusion. Its Groovy DSL uses an `exclude` block on the dependency declaration, followed by a separate `implementation` declaration for Jetty. Gradle can define broader configuration-level exclusions too, but that wider rule affects more dependency paths and should be used only when that is the intended policy. `dependencies` and `dependencyInsight` help explain what remains and why.

The replacement is not a ceremonial extra line. A normal executable servlet application needs a `ServletWebServerFactory`. With Tomcat removed and Jetty present, Boot's server auto-configuration can use the Jetty classes on the classpath. If no embedded server remains, an application that expects to run as an executable web server cannot start that server. A WAR deployed to an external servlet container has a different packaging arrangement, so the correct replacement depends on how the application is run.

Exclusions should follow evidence. A dependency might be removed because the application is switching servers, replacing a logging backend, or avoiding an artifact it truly does not use. Version alignment is usually handled through dependency management or Gradle constraints rather than by excluding an arbitrary version. After the change, compile the project, inspect the graph, start the relevant application mode, and run a request-level test.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: Inspect the graph before editing it: Maven dependency:tree or Gradle dependencies/dependencyInsight.
Put a Maven or Gradle exclusion on the dependency path that introduces the module.
A second path can still bring the same module into the final graph.
Add the intended replacement when the excluded dependency supplied required runtime behavior.
Verify the resolved graph and an application-level behavior after the swap.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A transitive exclusion tells the build tool not to follow one dependency edge. I first inspect the graph to find the direct dependency that brings the unwanted module. In Maven I place an `<exclusion>` with the module's group and artifact inside that dependency. In Gradle I attach `exclude group: ..., module: ...` to the dependency declaration.

For a Boot 3.3.1 web application switching from Tomcat to Jetty, I exclude `spring-boot-starter-tomcat` from `spring-boot-starter-web` and add `spring-boot-starter-jetty`. The web starter still supplies Spring MVC; the server implementation changes. With Jetty classes present, Boot can configure Jetty as the embedded servlet server. Excluding Tomcat without any replacement is wrong for an executable servlet application that still expects an embedded server.

The exclusion is path-scoped. If another dependency also brings Tomcat, it can remain in the final graph, so I verify with `mvn dependency:tree` or Gradle `dependencyInsight` rather than trusting the build file by sight. Gradle also allows wider configuration exclusions, but those have a larger effect than a per-dependency rule.

Finally, I compile, start the application in its real packaging mode, and run an HTTP check. I use dependency management or constraints for ordinary version alignment; exclusion is for removing an unwanted module or performing a deliberate replacement. That makes the classpath change visible, testable, and reversible.

sections.title: Maven and Gradle Exclusion Rules
sections.content:
| Concern | Maven | Gradle |
|---|---|---|
| Inspect graph | `mvn dependency:tree` | `dependencies` or `dependencyInsight` |
| Per-path exclusion | `<exclusions>` inside a dependency | `exclude` on a dependency declaration |
| Coordinates | `groupId` + `artifactId` | `group` + `module` |
| Wider policy | Add exclusions to every relevant path or enforce a rule | Configuration-level exclusions are available |
| Replacement | Add a separate dependency | Add a separate dependency |

sections.title: Replace Tomcat with Jetty
sections.content:
```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
    <exclusions>
        <exclusion>
            <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
            <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
        </exclusion>
    </exclusions>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-jetty</artifactId>
</dependency>
```

```groovy
dependencies {
    implementation('org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-web') {
        exclude group: 'org.springframework.boot',
                module: 'spring-boot-starter-tomcat'
    }
    implementation 'org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-jetty'
}
```

After resolving, the server branch should contain Jetty and no Tomcat path. If Tomcat remains, dependency insight should reveal the other incoming path that also needs a deliberate decision.

sections.title: Exclusion Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Editing before inspecting**: an exclusion on the wrong parent does not remove the actual path.
- **Assuming the module is globally gone**: another dependency path can still bring it in.
- **Removing a required implementation without replacement**: executable servlet applications still need an embedded server.
- **Using exclusion to solve every version disagreement**: dependency management and constraints are the normal alignment tools.
- **Stopping after a successful compile**: server swaps and logging swaps need runtime checks.
